Case
kās
n. (a condition or situation; a matter at law; in the phrase in any case, without exception)
Latin casus, a falling out, an occurrence — how a thing falls. The Authorized Version uses it both for a man's condition and for a legal matter, and the phrase in any case renders a Hebrew infinitive absolute meaning thou shalt surely do it.

Biblical Definition

“When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?” (Joh 5:6). Thirty-eight years by the pool, and the Lord knew the length of it before He asked. The question is not cruel; it is the necessary question to a man who had built a life around a condition and had an explanation ready instead of an answer. Deuteronomy uses the word for the law's hard cases — “this is the case of the slayer, which shall flee thither, that he may live” (Deu 19:4), the manslayer who killed ignorantly and whom the cities of refuge existed to protect from the avenger. And twice the law uses in any case to close every loophole: the straying ox must be brought back — “thou shalt in any case bring them again unto thy brother” (Deu 22:1) — and the poor man's pledge must be returned by sundown, “that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee: and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God” (Deu 24:13). Our Lord uses the same absolute form: “except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:20). And the psalmist ends the catalogue of national prosperity with the correction: “Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD” (Psa 144:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines case as literally that which falls or comes; hence a state of things, a condition; and in law, a cause or suit brought for decision.

expand to see more

CASE, n. Literally, that which falls, comes or happens; an event.

1. State of things; condition; as, the case of the sick man is desperate.

2. In law, a cause or suit in court; a statement of facts for the opinion of counsel.

3. Contingency; a supposed event; as, in case of failure.

IN ANY CASE, at all events; certainly; without exception.

Key Scripture

John 5:6 — "When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?"

Deu 24:13 — "In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down, that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee: and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God."

Mat 5:20 — "For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven."

Psa 144:15 — "Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Long affliction becomes an identity to be defended; our Lord asks a man of thirty-eight years whether he wills to be made whole.

expand to see more

John 5:6 asks a question the modern ear finds almost offensive, and it is worth sitting with rather than softening. Our Lord knew the man had been a long time in that case, and asked anyway: Wilt thou be made whole? The man's answer was not yes but an explanation of why it had never happened. Prolonged trouble can become the shape of a life — the way one is known, excused and understood — and healing then costs something. Nothing here mocks genuine affliction; the Lord healed him. But the question stands over every besetting condition that has quietly become a settled address.

The second recovery is the absolute in any case of the law. The straying ox goes back even if the brother is disliked; the poor man's coat goes back before sundown even though he still owes the money. The law refuses the exemptions we invent, and it attaches an unexpected promise: that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee: and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the LORD thy God. The debtor sleeping warm is counted to the creditor as righteousness. Mercy in small transactions is treated by God as a serious moral act.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar (H1697), a matter; the infinitive absolute construction rendered in any case; Greek ou me (G3756, G3361), the emphatic double negative — in no case.

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a case at law; Deuteronomy 19:4, the case of the slayer.

Hebrew infinitive absolute — the doubled verb (shob teshibem, returning thou shalt return them) rendered in any case; Deuteronomy 22:1, 24:13.

Hebrew 'abot (H5667) — a pledge, a pawn; the poor man's garment held for a debt.

Greek ou me (G3756 with G3361) — the emphatic double negative; Matthew 5:20, in no case enter into the kingdom.

Greek hugies (G5199) — whole, sound, healthy; John 5:6, wilt thou be made whole?

Usage

"“A long time in that case” — thirty-eight years, and He asked anyway."

"“In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge again” — before sundown."

"“Happy is that people, whose God is the LORD” — the correction to the catalogue."
